Review of Last Class

The Model, Recapped

\[C(x,y,z) = \frac{Q}{2\pi u\sigma_y\sigma_z}\exp\left(\frac{-y^2}{2\sigma_y^2}\right)\left[\exp\left(\frac{-(z-H)^2}{2\sigma_z^2}\right) + \exp\left(\frac{-(z+H)^2}{2\sigma_z^2}\right)\right]\]

Built from a real Péclet argument (drop along-wind dispersion) and a real boundary condition (ground reflection, verified numerically to cancel the vertical flux).

What Wednesday Left Open

We computed one number: the centreline concentration at 3 km.

A permit does not ask for one number. It asks where the worst point is, how much is there, and how large the region above the limit is.

Three Views of One Plume

Three Slices, One Function

\(C(x,y,z)\) is defined everywhere. We can only ever look at slices of it:

  • Plan view, \(z = 0\): the footprint on the ground, which is what a standard applies to.
  • Vertical section, \(y = 0\): how the plume gets from the stack down to the ground.
  • Crosswind profile, fixed \(x\): how wide it is where you are standing.

The Ground-Level Footprint

Code 
downwind_positions = 0.05:0.02:8.0
crosswind_positions = -700:5:700
footprint = [plume_ugm3(x, y, 0.0, plume_params) for y in crosswind_positions, x in downwind_positions]

p_foot = contourf(downwind_positions, crosswind_positions, footprint,
    color=:viridis, linewidth=0, clims=(0, 2000),
    xlabel="Distance downwind  [km]", ylabel="Crosswind distance  [m]")
plot!(p_foot, size=(1050, 450), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=10mm,
    bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm)

Reading the Footprint

The axes are not to scale. The plume is kilometres long and a few hundred metres wide.

Nothing reaches the ground for the first few hundred metres — the plume is still aloft at 41 m and has not spread down to \(z = 0\) yet.

Sigma Sets the Width

\(\sigma_y\) at 1 km: 34 m. At 8 km: 218 m.

Close to the stack it is smaller still — 4.3 m at 100 m downwind.

The plume spans two orders of magnitude in width across one domain. Remember that number.

The Plume in Section

Code 
heights = 0:2:200
section_positions = 0.2:0.02:8.0
section = [plume_ugm3(x, 0.0, z, plume_params) for z in heights, x in section_positions]

# Immediately above the stack the plume is a few metres across and the
# concentration there is enormous. Cap the scale at the ground-level range so
# the descent to the ground stays visible instead of being washed out.
p_section = contourf(section_positions, heights, section, color=:viridis, linewidth=0,
    clims=(0, 2000), xlabel="Distance downwind  [km]", ylabel="Height  [m]")
hline!(p_section, [plume_params.H], color=:white, linewidth=2, linestyle=:dash,
    label="stack height", legend=:topright)
plot!(p_section, size=(1050, 430), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=10mm,
    bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm)

The Peak Isn’t at the Stack

Code 
centerline_positions = 0.05:0.01:8.0
centerline = [plume_ugm3(x, 0.0, 0.0, plume_params) for x in centerline_positions]
peak_value, peak_index = findmax(centerline)
peak_distance = centerline_positions[peak_index]

p_line = plot(centerline_positions, centerline, color=:black, linewidth=4,
    xlabel="Distance downwind  [km]", ylabel="Ground-level centreline C  [µg/m³]",
    legend=false)
scatter!(p_line, [peak_distance], [peak_value], color=cb_vermillion, markersize=9)
plot!(p_line, size=(1050, 420), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=8mm,
    bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm)

Peak of 1747.0 µg/m³ at 2.46 km.

The same lesson as the DO sag curve: the worst point is downstream of the source, not at it.

The Grid Is a Choice

The Samples Are Exact

Every number in those figures is the exact solution of the plume equation at that point. There is no truncation error here at all.

And yet the answer you report still depends on the grid. Not because the samples are wrong — because of where they fall.

A Grid Can Step Over the Plume

At the peak distance the plume is only 76 m wide.

  • Crosswind spacing of 400 m reports 736.0 µg/m³
  • Crosswind spacing of 10 m reports 1743.0 µg/m³

The coarse grid is not slightly wrong. It is 42% of the right answer, because no sample landed near the centreline.

Sigma Sets the Spacing

In Week 4 the step size had to sit well inside the shortest characteristic timescale in the system.

Here the spacing has to sit well inside the smallest \(\sigma_y\) over the region you care about — and \(\sigma_y\) varies a hundredfold across this domain.

A grid that comfortably resolves the plume at 8 km steps straight over it at 100 m.

What You Should Report

Same recipe as the sag curve:

  1. Name the quantity you actually care about — peak, location, area above a limit.
  2. Halve the spacing until that quantity stops moving.
  3. Say what you did and what it changed.

The grid you chose changed the number you report to the regulator. That belongs in the report.

Key Takeaways and Upcoming Schedule

Key Takeaways

  • The ground-level footprint peaks downwind of the stack — the DO sag curve in a new geometry.
  • The vertical section shows the image term working: the plume piles up against the ground rather than passing through it.
  • The samples are exact; what you compute from them is not. A grid that misses the centreline reports a small fraction of the true peak.
  • \(\sigma_y\) sets the spacing, exactly as the characteristic timescale set \(\Delta t\).
